observations.text: The process starts when a customer sends us a request for a quotation. We take that request, prepare the quotation, and send it back to the customer by email. The intended outcome is to provide an accurate quotation that reflects the customer’s needs and our pricing.

I’m the one who prepares the quotations. When a request comes in, I record it, check the customer’s information in our CRM, and then create the quotation in our quoting system using the customer and pricing information. That’s the main tool I use for putting the quotation together.

When I check the customer information in the CRM, I’m mainly looking to confirm that the details are correct and up to date, like the customer’s name, contact info, and any relevant account details. If something is missing or looks incorrect, I’ll usually reach out to the customer or check internally to get the right information before I proceed with the quotation. I don’t have any special conditions or branches beyond that—I just make sure the info is accurate before creating the quote.

The pricing information comes from our quoting system—it’s already set up there based on our standard pricing. When I create the quotation, I use that pricing information as it appears in the system. I don’t determine the price myself; I just apply what’s in the system for the customer and the products or services they’re asking about.

Normally, once I’ve created the quotation in the system, I send it to the customer by email. There isn’t any special review or approval step in the usual flow—I just make sure the quotation is accurate and then send it off.

Checking the customer’s information in the CRM is necessary because we need to make sure we’re quoting the right customer and using the correct details. If I skipped it, there’s a risk the quotation could go to the wrong person or contain outdated information, which could cause problems later. It’s just a way to keep things accurate before we send anything out.

Creating the quotation in the quoting system is necessary because that’s where the pricing and the actual quote are put together. Without that step, we wouldn’t have a proper, standardized quotation to send to the customer. It also keeps a record of the quote in the system, which is useful for tracking and reference.

Sending the quotation by email is necessary because that’s how the customer actually receives the quote. Without that step, the quotation wouldn’t reach them, and the whole process wouldn’t be complete. It’s the final part of getting the accurate quotation into the customer’s hands.

Recording the incoming request is necessary because it gives us a clear record that the request was made and helps us keep track of what we’re working on. It also makes it easier to follow up or refer back to if there are any questions later. Without that step, we might lose track of requests or miss something.

It’s necessary because if the customer information is missing or incorrect, we can’t be sure we’re quoting the right person or using the right details. Reaching out to the customer or checking internally helps us get accurate information so the quotation is correct and goes to the right place. Without that step, we’d risk sending a quote based on wrong or incomplete details.

Yes, there is one exception. For quotations over 1,000,000 yen, we need approval from a manager before the quotation is sent. That approval is for credit risk management. Otherwise, the process is the same as what I described.
